name: Kubernetes
summary: The standard open-source orchestrator: declare the containers you want, and controllers keep the cluster matching it.
intro: A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane (an API server backed by the etcd key-value store, a scheduler and a set of controllers) and worker nodes, each running an agent called the kubelet. You submit objects to the API, such as a Deployment that asks for three replicas of a Pod. The scheduler picks a node with enough free CPU and memory for each Pod, the kubelet starts its containers, and controllers keep comparing what exists with what you asked for, replacing Pods that crash or whose node disappears.

Google open-sourced Kubernetes in 2014, and it is now run by the CNCF. Its real difference from simpler orchestrators is the API itself: everything (load-balanced Services, config, secrets, storage volumes, batch Jobs) is a declarative object, and you can add your own object types with controllers that manage them. That is why databases, autoscalers and deploy tools ship as Kubernetes “operators”, and why every major cloud sells a managed version (EKS, GKE, AKS).
strengths: Self-healing, rolling updates and rollbacks, service discovery and bin packing built in
Runs the same way on every cloud and on your own hardware
Extensible API: custom resources and operators let other tools plug in as first-class objects
Designed for clusters of up to 5,000 nodes and 150,000 Pods
limits: Many moving parts: networking, ingress, storage, upgrades and RBAC all need expertise
The control plane and per-node agents cost money and attention even for a tiny app
It doesn’t add or remove machines on its own; you need a node autoscaler such as Karpenter
Containers on a node share its kernel, so mixing untrusted tenants needs extra sandboxing, such as gVisor or Kata Containers through a RuntimeClass

snippet.title: A Deployment that keeps three replicas running

story: Google had started experimenting with containers more than a decade earlier to squeeze more work out of its servers, and ran them across huge clusters with an internal system called Borg and later its successor, Omega. Outside, Docker had just made containers easy to build and run on one machine in 2013, but there was no common way to run them across a fleet of machines. Meanwhile customers of Google Compute Engine were paying for a lot of CPUs with “extremely low” utilisation, because they were running whole VMs.

In summer 2013 Craig McLuckie, Joe Beda and Brendan Burns pitched Urs Hölzle, Google’s head of technical infrastructure, on a container manager for everyone else, built on Borg and Omega’s lessons; Eric Brewer helped win approval. Its codename, Project Seven of Nine, a nod to Borg via Star Trek, is why the Kubernetes logo has seven sides. The first commit landed on June 6, 2014, and the project was unveiled at DockerCon that month. Version 1.0 shipped on July 21, 2015, and Google worked with the Linux Foundation to create the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, with Kubernetes as its founding project.

Kubernetes became the common layer for running containers: Microsoft and AWS announced managed versions in 2017, and an ecosystem of tools is built on its API. It even outgrew Docker, dropping its built-in Docker support in version 1.24 (2022).

choices.choice: Declare the desired state; controllers converge on it
choices.why: You store what you want, and independent controllers keep comparing it with what exists. They react to the current state rather than to individual events, so a missed message or crashed component heals itself on the next pass.

choices.choice: Every Pod gets its own IP address
choices.why: When apps share a machine’s IP they must coordinate ports, which the docs call “very difficult to do at scale”. One IP per Pod lets every app use the port it expects, at the cost of more networking work.

choices.choice: Built-in features use the same API as add-ons
choices.why: Kubernetes exposes the same interfaces it uses itself, so custom resources and controllers (“operators”) can teach it about databases or certificates as if they were native objects.

choices.choice: Open source, then a neutral foundation
choices.why: The founders wanted instant feedback and engineers from businesses that would actually deploy containers. Handing it to the CNCF in 2015 put it under neutral governance rather than Google’s alone.

timeline.text: McLuckie, Beda and Burns pitch the project inside Google
First commit on June 6; unveiled at DockerCon
Version 1.0 on July 21; donated to the newly formed CNCF
Microsoft (AKS) and AWS (EKS) announce managed Kubernetes
Version 1.24 removes the built-in Docker shim
